title: The iqamah
hookLine: the second call, just before prayer begins

lines: ROWS WHERE THERE WAS A CROWD.
cards: Inside a mosque, a few minutes after the adhan. The room is loose and quiet. A teenager scrolls his phone by the wall.
Two old friends murmur near the back. Someone prays a couple of units alone in a corner. A boy ties and reties his shoelace for no reason.
Then a man near the front stands and starts a second call, quicker than the first, flatter, almost brisk. And the whole room changes shape. Phones go into pockets.
People rise, step forward, line up shoulder to shoulder, and close the gaps between them. By the time he finishes, there are rows where there was a crowd.

teach.h: THE ADHAN FOR THE STREET, THE IQAMAH FOR THE ROOM.
teach.b: That second call is the iqamah. The adhan goes out to the street: the time has come, wherever you are, come. The iqamah is for the room: the prayer is starting, here, now.

Its words mostly follow the adhan, and Sahih al-Bukhari, number 605, records how Bilal was told to say them: the adhan's phrases in pairs, the iqamah's singly, except for one new line that the adhan doesn't have.

teach.h: QAD QAMATI AS-SALAH: IT HAS BEGUN.
teach.b: Qad qamati as-salah. The prayer has stood up. It has begun.
The Hanafi school says the iqamah's phrases in pairs, like the adhan, and the other Sunni schools say most of them singly; each follows reports it trusts. Between the two calls there's a space.

teach.h: BETWEEN THE TWO CALLS, A PRAYER.
teach.b: In Sahih al-Bukhari, number 624, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says that between every two calls there is a prayer, for whoever wants it: a waiting room with a door already open.
And how should you arrive when you hear the iqamah? A sprint might seem right. The hadith says the opposite.
Sahih al-Bukhari, number 636: when you hear the iqamah, walk to the prayer with calm and dignity, don't hurry; whatever you catch, pray it, and whatever you missed, complete it afterward.
So the call that says now doesn't mean panic. It means stand, step in, and join the row as you are. The adhan gathers people from far away.
The iqamah gathers the people already in the room into one line.

how: In the mosque, someone calls the iqamah just before the congregational prayer starts; the worshipers stand, form straight rows behind the imam, and the prayer begins. It may also be said by someone about to pray alone.

p: for the street: the time has come
for the room: it begins now

when you hear the iqamah, the hadith says run
Bukhari 636: walk with calm and dignity, pray what you catch, complete what you missed.

games.q: you're walking up to the mosque and you hear the iqamah start inside. you might miss the beginning. what does the hadith say to do?
o: run, so you don't miss anything.
walk in calmly, join, and complete what you missed after.
games.why: Bukhari 636: walk with calm and dignity, don't hurry. pray what you catch, and complete what you missed.

practice: If you're sitting, notice the looseness of waiting first; then, without rushing, stand and feel your feet take your weight, your shoulders settle, your hands rest.
Stay standing, or sit again if you need to, and breathe slowly in the space after the call.
If you pray, you can stand this way at your next prayer, calm, not hurried; if not, this is simply the difference between waiting and beginning.

wordCard.voice: Iqamah. The second call, said in the room just before the prayer begins, with its own line: the prayer has stood up. Today's word.
